title: BGP routing and origin validation
heading: Select a route, then forward to the longest matching prefix
problem: two decisions made at different stages: choosing a BGP route for one prefix and forwarding a packet among installed prefixes.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='bgp-routing-title' viewBox='0 0 720 407'><title id='bgp-routing-title'>Select a route, then forward to the longest matching prefix</title><g font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' fill='#17343d' font-size='19'><rect x='22' y='18' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='43' font-weight='600'>1. Validate and apply import policy</text><text x='40' y='67' font-size='17'>Check origin authorization and local acceptance rules.</text><path d='M360 81 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='96' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='121' font-weight='600'>2. Choose a route for the same prefix</text><text x='40' y='145' font-size='17'>Higher LOCAL_PREF wins before a shorter AS_PATH in this model.</text><path d='M360 159 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='174' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='199' font-weight='600'>3. Install the selected route</text><text x='40' y='223' font-size='17'>The forwarding table can contain /16 and /24 entries together.</text><path d='M360 237 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='252' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='277' font-weight='600'>4. Forward a destination packet</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>Use the longest matching installed prefix, such as /24.</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Policy chooses a route; prefix length chooses a forwarding entry.</text></g></svg>
explanation: An autonomous system (AS) is a network under a common routing administration. Its AS number identifies it in interdomain routing. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) advertises reachable IP prefixes between ASes. The AS_PATH lists the ASes a route advertisement has traversed; a receiver can reject a path containing its own AS to prevent a routing loop.

An AS may pay a provider for transit, exchange traffic with a peer, or receive payment from a customer. These relationships motivate import and export policies. LOCAL_PREF is a local preference value used inside an AS: a larger value usually wins when comparing acceptable routes to the same prefix. If those values tie, a shorter AS_PATH can become the next deciding attribute. Real decision processes have additional checks and tie breakers.

A prefix identifies an address block. In IPv4, /p fixes p of 32 address bits, leaving 2^(32-p) addresses. A router can select and install a route for 198.18.0.0/16 and another for 198.18.4.0/24. A packet to 198.18.4.9 matches both, so longest-prefix matching uses /24. LOCAL_PREF comparisons happened earlier, separately for each prefix.

A prefix hijack advertises reachability without the intended authorization. A more-specific announcement can attract traffic through longest-prefix matching if routers accept and install it. A route leak exports a route beyond the permitted business relationship, whether caused by an error or deliberate action. Both can redirect traffic; encryption and authentication at higher layers still determine whether redirected application data can be read or impersonated.

Address allocation passes through IANA, regional Internet registries and their delegated registries or network operators. Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) uses this resource hierarchy to support signed Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs). A validated ROA authorizes an origin AS for a prefix and a maximum announcement length. Route Origin Validation (ROV) labels a route Valid when a covering authorization permits both its origin and length, Invalid when a covering authorization exists but none permits both, and NotFound when no covering authorization exists. Local policy decides how to treat each result.

ROV checks the claimed origin, rather than every intermediate AS_PATH hop or export relationship. BGPsec adds signed path propagation; provider-relationship mechanisms such as ASPA target different policy evidence. Fig. 2 lets you separate same-prefix route preference from destination forwarding. Its simplified policy order illustrates these decisions and omits vendor-specific tie breakers.
example: A ROA authorizes origin AS 64500 for 198.18.0.0/16 with maxLength 24. An announcement of 198.18.4.0/24 by AS 64500 is origin-valid; a /25 exceeds this authorization. For two accepted /24 routes with LOCAL_PREF 180 and 90, the route with 180 wins even if its AS_PATH is longer.

questions.prompt: Two accepted routes to 198.18.4.0/24 have LOCAL_PREF 160 with four AS hops and LOCAL_PREF 80 with two hops. Which route wins under the stated policy, and what changes if an accepted /25 is also installed for the packet destination?
questions.hint: Separate selection among routes to /24 from forwarding among different installed prefixes.
questions.answer: For /24, LOCAL_PREF 160 wins before AS_PATH length is considered. A destination matching an installed /25 uses that /25 entry through longest-prefix matching. Its selection was a separate per-prefix decision.

questions.prompt: A ROA permits 198.18.0.0/16, maxLength 24, origin AS 64500. Classify a /24 by AS 64501 and a /25 by AS 64500. What can you conclude about intermediate hops in a Valid route?
questions.hint: Check authorized origin and allowed length independently.
questions.answer: Both announcements are Invalid given this sole covering ROA: the /24 has the wrong origin and the /25 is too specific. A Valid result authenticates the origin authorization, while intermediate path hops and export policies require other evidence.

title: TCP sequence and acknowledgement numbers
heading: Track two independent byte streams in opposite directions
problem: a browser request and a server reply, with each sequence number belonging to its sender and each acknowledgement referring to the other sender.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='tcp-sequence-space-title' viewBox='0 0 720 407'><title id='tcp-sequence-space-title'>Track two independent byte streams in opposite directions</title><g font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' fill='#17343d' font-size='19'><rect x='22' y='18' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='43' font-weight='600'>Browser → server</text><text x='40' y='67' font-size='17'>SEQ = 4000, ACK = 9000, payload = 80 bytes</text><path d='M360 81 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='96' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='121' font-weight='600'>Server receives bytes 4000 through 4079</text><text x='40' y='145' font-size='17'>Next browser byte expected: 4080</text><path d='M360 159 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='174' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='199' font-weight='600'>Server → browser</text><text x='40' y='223' font-size='17'>SEQ = 9000, ACK = 4080, payload = 24 bytes</text><path d='M360 237 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='252' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='277' font-weight='600'>After that reply is received</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>Browser expects server byte 9024 next</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Assume in-order data, an established connection, and no SYN or FIN.</text></g></svg>
explanation: TCP presents applications with a reliable, ordered byte stream in each direction. A connection is identified by source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port, often called its four-tuple. Each endpoint numbers the bytes it sends. The browser and server therefore keep two separate sequence spaces, even though their traffic shares a connection.

SEQ in a segment identifies the first payload byte carried by that sender. ACK identifies the next sequence number that sender expects from its peer. An ACK of 4080 cumulatively acknowledges all preceding bytes through 4079, assuming a continuous received stream. ACK numbers travel in the reverse direction from the bytes they acknowledge.

For an accepted in-order segment starting at sequence s with L payload bytes, the next expected number is s + L. More generally its sequence-space length is L + S + F, where S is 1 when SYN is set and F is 1 when FIN is set, otherwise each is 0. SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. A pure ACK has L = S = F = 0 and consumes none. IP, TCP and link headers do not count as TCP payload bytes.

During connection setup, the client chooses an initial sequence number x and the server independently chooses y. The initial SYN has SEQ x. The SYN-ACK has SEQ y and ACK x+1. The final empty ACK has SEQ x+1 and ACK y+1. Thus x and y come from the endpoints, rather than from packet sizes or from one another. Implementations choose initial values to make blind prediction harder.

Once data flows, advance only the sequence space that carried those bytes. In Fig. 1 the browser sends 80 bytes, advancing the server’s ACK by 80. The server’s own SEQ starts at 9000 because the browser was already expecting that server byte. The server’s 24-byte reply advances its next SEQ to 9024 after sending. It does not change the ACK of browser bytes unless more browser data arrives.

A lost section of the stream stops cumulative ACK progress. If bytes 1000–1099 and 1200–1299 arrive while 1100–1199 are missing, the receiver still ACKs 1100. Selective acknowledgement can additionally report later received ranges. Fig. 2 uses in-order delivery without retransmissions or sequence-number wraparound; actual TCP sequence arithmetic is modulo 2^32.
example: An established client sends SEQ 7200, ACK 15000 and 60 payload bytes. With no other traffic, the server replies with SEQ 15000 and ACK 7260. If its reply carries 40 bytes, its next fresh data SEQ is 15040; the client’s next data SEQ remains 7260.

questions.prompt: A client sends SEQ 12000, ACK 45000 and 90 payload bytes. The server immediately replies with 30 payload bytes. Give the server’s SEQ and ACK and the client’s ACK after receiving the reply. Assume in-order delivery with no SYN, FIN or other traffic.
questions.hint: Place client bytes and server bytes on separate number lines.
questions.answer: The server uses SEQ 45000 and ACK 12090. Its reply covers server bytes 45000–45029, so the client then ACKs 45030. The 90 client bytes affect the acknowledgement of client data; the 30 server bytes affect the acknowledgement of server data.

questions.prompt: Client SYN has SEQ 700 and server SYN-ACK has SEQ 9800. Give the final empty ACK’s SEQ and ACK, then the server’s ACK after the client sends its first 12 data bytes.
questions.hint: Each SYN consumes one sequence number before the data starts.
questions.answer: The final ACK uses SEQ 701 and ACK 9801. The client’s first data bytes are 701–712, so the server acknowledges 713. The empty final ACK itself consumed no sequence number.

sourceNotes: Course sequence: Transport Layer Security; original byte-ledger examples complement packet-capture reasoning.

title: TCP injection and disruption
heading: Separate transport acceptance from cryptographic acceptance
problem: an injected packet passing through two different checks: TCP stream processing and TLS record authentication.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='tcp-attacks-title' viewBox='0 0 720 407'><title id='tcp-attacks-title'>Separate transport acceptance from cryptographic acceptance</title><g font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' fill='#17343d' font-size='19'><rect x='22' y='18' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='43' font-weight='600'>1. Attacker guesses or observes connection fields</text><text x='40' y='67' font-size='17'>Source/destination IPs, ports and sequence state</text><path d='M360 81 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='96' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='121' font-weight='600'>2. TCP processes an acceptable segment</text><text x='40' y='145' font-size='17'>Receive-window and connection-state rules apply</text><path d='M360 159 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='174' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='199' font-weight='600'>3. TLS verifies the recovered protected record</text><text x='40' y='223' font-size='17'>Valid authentication is required for plaintext delivery</text><path d='M360 237 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='252' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='277' font-weight='600'>4. Application receives authenticated data</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>Packet dropping or connection resets can still interrupt service</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>A TCP checksum detects transmission errors; TLS authenticates records.</text></g></svg>
explanation: TCP supplies ordering and recovery over IP. Its checksum catches many accidental bit errors, while its connection fields and sequence numbers organize delivery. An attacker who can construct packets with the right visible values can also compute a valid checksum. Cryptographic evidence of a trusted sender must come from an additional protection such as TLS or IPsec.

An on-path observer can see ordinary TCP addresses, ports and sequence numbers. It can drop or delay packets and may attempt to inject a forged segment in the receive window. A blind off-path attacker has to infer or guess the connection fields and acceptable sequence state. Random source ports and unpredictable initial sequence numbers increase that guessing work.

An accepted forged RST can abort a connection. Modern TCP reset validation is state-dependent: an exact next expected sequence number can terminate an established connection, while some in-window reset guesses trigger a challenge ACK. Describing an attack therefore requires the attacker’s visibility, endpoint state and implementation rules, rather than the RST flag alone.

For payload injection, TCP may accept stream bytes before the application protocol evaluates them. TLS record authentication then checks that the bytes match the negotiated keys, record context and authentication tag. Fabricated bytes fail that check unless the attacker has suitable key material or exploits a specific flaw. Authentication failure or missing bytes can still interrupt the session.

UDP sends independent datagrams without a TCP handshake or ordered stream. Its checksum likewise does not authenticate a sender. Applications using UDP must define their own matching, replay and reliability rules as needed. DNS adds a query/reply matching problem; QUIC adds authenticated transport state and recovery over UDP.
example: A network attacker can observe an HTTPS connection and inject a correctly checksummed TCP packet. If TCP accepts those bytes but they alter a TLS ciphertext record, the receiver’s TLS authentication fails. The attacker has gained disruption in this example; producing a chosen authenticated application message requires a further cryptographic capability.

questions.prompt: An on-path attacker sees TCP sequence numbers but lacks the TLS traffic keys. Describe one feasible service disruption and explain the validation stage that protects application message authenticity.
questions.hint: Follow Fig. 1 from packet arrival through plaintext delivery.
questions.answer: The attacker can drop packets or try a reset meeting TCP’s state-dependent acceptance rules. Forged TLS record content fails cryptographic authentication, preventing its release as an authenticated application message. Availability remains exposed to packet loss and transport disruption.

questions.prompt: Why does a valid TCP checksum alone provide weak evidence that a segment came from the intended peer?
questions.hint: Ask which required input is secret.
questions.answer: The checksum is computed from public header and payload fields with no secret key. An attacker constructing a packet can calculate it too. A keyed authenticator or authenticated channel provides sender-related cryptographic evidence.

sourceNotes: Course sequence: Transport Layer Security, TCP threats and UDP properties.
RFC 9293, TCP state and checksum: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html

title: DNS resolution and forged-reply races
heading: Follow a name lookup before evaluating a cache-poisoning attempt
problem: a resolver obtaining an answer through delegated authority and caching that answer for later clients.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='dns-cache-title' viewBox='0 0 720 407'><title id='dns-cache-title'>Follow a name lookup before evaluating a cache-poisoning attempt</title><g font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' fill='#17343d' font-size='19'><rect x='22' y='18' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='43' font-weight='600'>Client → recursive resolver</text><text x='40' y='67' font-size='17'>Ask for the A record of portal.example</text><path d='M360 81 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='96' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='121' font-weight='600'>Resolver → root, then parent, then authority</text><text x='40' y='145' font-size='17'>Follow referrals until the responsible zone answers</text><path d='M360 159 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='174' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='199' font-weight='600'>Reply matching and cache acceptance</text><text x='40' y='223' font-size='17'>Check question, peer addresses, ports, ID and relevant authority</text><path d='M360 237 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='252' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='277' font-weight='600'>Cached answer → client</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>TTL bounds reuse; a poisoned accepted answer can affect later lookups</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>A cache hit can avoid the upstream lookup and its reply race.</text></g></svg>
explanation: DNS maps names to typed records. An A record carries an IPv4 address, AAAA an IPv6 address, CNAME an alias, NS a zone’s authoritative server name and MX a mail destination. A record’s time to live (TTL), measured in seconds, limits how long a resolver can reuse it from a cache. A client usually asks a recursive resolver to perform the work.

On a cache miss, the resolver can make iterative queries: a root points toward the top-level domain, that parent points toward the child zone, and the authoritative server returns the requested data. A referral can carry glue addresses needed to reach an in-zone nameserver. Bailiwick and credibility rules restrict which accompanying records can influence the cache; arbitrary unrelated Additional-section data does not gain authority merely by arriving in a reply.

For a conventional UDP exchange, a resolver matches a response to an outstanding question and expected server, addresses, ports and 16-bit transaction ID. A blind attacker races forged responses against the legitimate one. A guessed ID helps only if the rest of the matching and acceptance conditions also hold. Source-port randomization adds uncertainty when those ports remain unpredictable through the network path.

For one outstanding query with b independent uniformly unknown bits and g independent random guesses before the legitimate reply, a simple model gives P(success) = 1 − (1 − 2^(−b))^g. Here b counts effective unknown ID and port bits, not nominal field widths. With small g/2^b, P ≈ g/2^b. Fig. 2 varies that toy race; real attacks also depend on timing, query concurrency, NAT behavior and resolver rules.

A cached legitimate response can suppress repeated upstream races for the same name until expiration. Attackers may induce fresh names to trigger new lookups and attempt to poison delegation data that affects a wider zone. The defense combines strict reply matching, unpredictable query values, careful cache policy and cryptographic validation where DNSSEC is deployed.

DNS over TLS (DoT) and DNS over HTTPS (DoH) protect a client’s channel to its chosen resolver. The resolver still observes those questions and determines the answers it returns. DNSSEC authenticates signed DNS data through a trust chain. These protections act at different boundaries and can be used together.
example: Assume one query, exactly 16 unpredictable ID bits, a known source port and 100 independent random forged guesses. The toy success probability is 1 − (65535/65536)^100 ≈ 0.001525, or 0.1525%. Adding 12 independent effective port bits makes b = 28 and the probability about 0.0000373%. These values describe the stated race, rather than a whole resolver’s security.

questions.prompt: In the toy model, an attacker gets 200 independent random guesses against one query with 20 effective unknown bits. Estimate success probability and state two assumptions that could change the result.
questions.hint: Use g/2^b when g is much smaller than 2^b.
questions.answer: P ≈ 200/1,048,576 = 0.0001907, or 0.0191%. The model assumes uniform independent unknown values, independent random guesses, one outstanding query, correct other reply fields and guesses arriving before the legitimate answer. Predictable ports, additional queries or a shorter race can change the result.

questions.prompt: A laptop uses DoH to a resolver that returns a fabricated unsigned address. Which trust boundary does DoH protect, and what additional evidence would DNSSEC validation require?
questions.hint: Identify the endpoint of encryption and the origin of the DNS data.
questions.answer: DoH authenticates and encrypts the laptop-to-resolver channel under its HTTPS trust model. DNSSEC validation requires a signed answer and a validated DNSKEY/DS chain to a configured trust anchor, or authenticated evidence describing an unsigned delegation. A secure channel alone does not make a resolver’s chosen data authoritative. An authenticated proof of an unsigned delegation establishes Insecure status; the unsigned A value itself remains unauthenticated, so this branch cannot detect that fabricated address.

title: DNSSEC chains and authenticated denial
heading: Authenticate DNS data through a chain of zone keys
problem: a validator connecting a trusted root key to a signed answer by checking each delegation and each signature.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='dnssec-validation-title' viewBox='0 0 720 407'><title id='dnssec-validation-title'>Authenticate DNS data through a chain of zone keys</title><g font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' fill='#17343d' font-size='19'><rect x='22' y='18' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='43' font-weight='600'>1. Configured trust anchor</text><text x='40' y='67' font-size='17'>Start with a trusted root DNSKEY or equivalent anchor</text><path d='M360 81 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='96' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='121' font-weight='600'>2. Parent authenticates a DS record</text><text x='40' y='145' font-size='17'>DS contains a digest identifying an authorized child key</text><path d='M360 159 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='174' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='199' font-weight='600'>3. Child DNSKEY set and answer signatures</text><text x='40' y='223' font-size='17'>Validate DNSKEY, then RRSIG over the requested RRset</text><path d='M360 237 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='252' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='277' font-weight='600'>4. Classify the result</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>Secure, insecure, bogus or indeterminate describes validation</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>An RRset groups records with the same owner name, type and class.</text></g></svg>
explanation: DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) add origin authentication and integrity to DNS data. An authoritative zone signs resource-record sets, called RRsets, and publishes the signatures in RRSIG records. A validating resolver verifies the signatures against authenticated public keys. The records remain readable to observers unless a separate encrypted transport protects the lookup.

A DNSKEY record publishes a zone key. A parent’s Delegation Signer (DS) record contains a digest of a child DNSKEY and identifies the authorized key and algorithms. The validator authenticates the parent’s DS, finds the matching child DNSKEY and validates the child DNSKEY RRset. That authenticated set provides keys for validating the child’s signed answer. Repeat from a configured trust anchor down the name hierarchy.

A zone may use separate key-signing and zone-signing roles to simplify rollover. Their operational jobs differ, while DNSKEY and signature validation establish the actual trust. Every step needs supported algorithms, acceptable signature time bounds, correct signed names/types and a successful cryptographic check. Possessing any self-signed public key for a name supplies no trusted delegation by itself.

A secure result has a successfully validated chain and signatures. An insecure result means authenticated delegation evidence establishes an unsigned branch where secure data was not expected. Bogus means data expected to validate fails, such as a broken signature or a missing required key. Indeterminate describes cases where validation status cannot be established from the available trust information. A validating resolver generally returns failure for bogus data instead of silently treating it as insecure.

An attacker could otherwise forge “no such name” to suppress a valid service. NSEC records authenticate an interval between existing names and list record types at an owner. NSEC3 uses hashed-name ordering to make straightforward zone enumeration harder, with its own disclosure and operational tradeoffs. These records give signed evidence for negative answers without requiring an online signing key to sign every invented query name.

A laptop relying on its recursive resolver must also trust how the validation result reaches it. An unauthenticated attacker on that final hop could replace an ordinary response, including a claimed AD flag. Local validation or an authenticated channel to a trusted validating resolver closes that particular gap. DNSSEC still leaves questions visible over unencrypted links and accepts an authorized zone operator’s chosen data.
example: The parent has a validated DS for key K1. The child supplies a different key K2, a self-signature under K2 and an A-record signature under K2. The answer fails the chain because K2 does not match the authenticated DS. Self-consistent signatures establish possession of K2, while the parent’s DS establishes which key is authorized.

questions.prompt: A signed child zone validates yesterday. Today its parent still publishes the old DS, but the child has removed every matching DNSKEY. How should a validator classify the answer, and why?
questions.hint: Trace the trust chain at the delegation before testing the answer signature.
questions.answer: The answer is bogus under the stated trust anchor and supported algorithms. The parent requires a signed child through its authenticated DS, but the validator cannot establish an authorized child key. A signature under a new unlinked key cannot complete the chain.

questions.prompt: Why does a DNSSEC validator need signed evidence for NXDOMAIN, and what does an NSEC-style proof establish?
questions.hint: Treat the absence claim as an answer an attacker might try to replace.
questions.answer: An attacker could forge an unsigned absence claim to hide a real name. A signed NSEC proof authenticates the relevant name interval and type information used to establish absence. The validator checks the signatures and proof conditions through the same trusted zone-key chain.

title: TLS identity and session keys
heading: Bind a fresh shared secret to the intended server
problem: the separate roles of key agreement, certificate authentication and handshake confirmation in a certificate-based TLS 1.3 session.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='tls-session-keys-title' viewBox='0 0 720 407'><title id='tls-session-keys-title'>Bind a fresh shared secret to the intended server</title><g font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' fill='#17343d' font-size='19'><rect x='22' y='18' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='43' font-weight='600'>Client → server: ClientHello</text><text x='40' y='67' font-size='17'>Supported choices and an ephemeral key share A</text><path d='M360 81 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='96' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='121' font-weight='600'>Server → client: ServerHello</text><text x='40' y='145' font-size='17'>Selected choices and an ephemeral key share B</text><path d='M360 159 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='174' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='199' font-weight='600'>Encrypted server authentication messages</text><text x='40' y='223' font-size='17'>Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished</text><path d='M360 237 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='252' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='277' font-weight='600'>Client verifies, then sends Finished</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>Traffic keys protect application records in each direction</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Selected message roles; optional client certificates and resumption omitted.</text></g></svg>
explanation: Transport Layer Security (TLS) provides an authenticated encrypted channel between endpoints. HTTPS uses that channel for HTTP. A browser wants both a secret session key and evidence that the peer controls a certificate authorized for its intended server name. The certificate names a public key; the handshake proves possession of the corresponding private key and binds it to this connection.

Ephemeral Diffie–Hellman contributes a fresh secret from each peer. In finite-field notation, let p be a prime, g a group generator and a and b private exponents. Public shares are A = g^a mod p and B = g^b mod p. The common value is Z = B^a mod p = A^b mod p. Modern TLS commonly uses elliptic-curve groups with the analogous shared-secret property. Small arithmetic examples explain the mechanism; deployed groups use approved parameters and validation.

The browser builds a certificate path to a locally trusted certification authority (CA), checks signatures, validity periods and constraints, and checks that the intended server identity matches an allowed certificate name. Its revocation policy can use certificate revocation lists, OCSP or other mechanisms. A chain that verifies cryptographically still needs the correct application identity and permitted key use.

TLS 1.3 CertificateVerify signs the handshake transcript with the certificate’s private key. This binds the server’s authenticated identity to the exchanged parameters and key shares. Finished authenticates the transcript under a derived handshake key, confirming the computed key material and handshake history. The client must complete the required checks before treating application data as authenticated from the intended server.

HKDF derives purpose-specific secrets and separate traffic keys for each direction from the shared material and transcript context. Fresh ephemeral contributions, erased after use, support forward secrecy: later theft of the server’s long-term signing key alone does not reveal recorded sessions’ erased ephemeral secrets. This property depends on the chosen exchange and handling of secrets.

TLS 1.2 also supports ephemeral (EC)DHE, with signed server key-exchange parameters and Finished checks. Its older RSA key-transport option encrypts a premaster secret under the certificate’s RSA key and lacks forward secrecy against later theft of that decryption key. A certificate using RSA for signatures can still authenticate an ephemeral exchange; the certificate key type alone does not identify the key-establishment method.
example: For algebra only, p = 23, g = 5, a = 6 and b = 15 give A = 8, B = 19 and Z = 2 at both endpoints. In TLS, the key schedule combines suitable shared material with transcript context to derive distinct traffic secrets. The server must still authenticate the exchange; an impersonator can perform its own unauthenticated key agreement.

questions.prompt: Why does proving that both ends computed a shared secret fail to establish the server's intended identity by itself?
questions.hint: An impersonator can participate in its own key exchange.
questions.answer: Key agreement alone identifies no trusted peer. Authentication must bind the transcript and key shares to the intended server, using the certificate/identity checks and proof of its private-key possession in this flow.

questions.prompt: Why derive traffic keys instead of directly treating the raw Diffie–Hellman value as every encryption key?
questions.hint: Consider extraction, protocol context, and separate key uses.
questions.answer: A key-derivation schedule converts the shared material into appropriate keys and separates their purposes and directions. HKDF's context inputs bind the outputs to their intended protocol use.

title: TLS records, downgrade paths and limits
heading: Identify the established channel before judging attacker capabilities
problem: a network attacker encountering certificate checks, authenticated records and an application’s HTTPS upgrade policy at different stages.

State the remaining attacker capability</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>Observe metadata, interrupt transport, or exploit a specified weakness</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Version, cipher suite, peer identity and fallback behavior are explicit inputs.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A browser request crosses routing, DNS and transport machinery before reaching its TLS peer. Poisoning DNS or redirecting packets can move the connection toward an attacker-controlled host. Certificate-name validation and handshake authentication still require proof for the intended site. An attacker with no acceptable credential can cause a failed connection or relay encrypted traffic, rather than automatically becoming the authenticated endpoint.

After a successful modern TLS handshake, record authentication detects changed or fabricated application ciphertext, and encryption protects the payload from a passive network observer. Record sequence and nonce rules bind protection to protocol state. Packet addresses, timing and approximate encrypted lengths remain observable at the network boundary. A peer endpoint, trusted interception proxy or compromised application sees plaintext at its own termination point.

TLS version and cipher suite specify the actual record mechanisms. TLS 1.3 uses AEAD suites and removes many legacy options. TLS 1.2 supports AEAD and also older constructions. TLS 1.1 is deprecated and predates those modern requirements; evaluating an alleged attack requires the negotiated suite, implementation and required attacker capability. Merely stating an older version supplies no universal decryption procedure.

A network attacker may drop handshake messages to provoke an application’s legacy retry behavior. Changing version fields within an authenticated handshake changes its transcript and should fail the required checks. TLS 1.3 includes downgrade-detection values in ServerHello.random when a capable server negotiates an older version, allowing capable clients to detect certain forced downgrades. Actual downgrade outcomes depend on both endpoints’ support and fallback policy.

HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) tells a browser to require HTTPS for a host for a stated time, with optional subdomain coverage. A previously learned policy or preloaded entry protects the initial HTTP choice. On a first visit without such a policy, an attacker may interfere with an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect and keep the user on HTTP if the application permits it. This is a change in whether TLS is used at all, with different assumptions from negotiating a TLS version.

Certificate revocation addresses credentials that should no longer be accepted before their expiry. Signed revocation evidence can be checked for authenticity even when transported over an untrusted channel, while freshness and availability still matter. TLS also relies on protected endpoints and correct user/application decisions about certificate errors. A network attacker can continue to drop packets or disrupt TCP even when record cryptography remains sound.

A certificate revocation list (CRL) is a signed list that clients can download and cache; its update times determine freshness. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) answers status queries for individual certificates. OCSP stapling lets the server deliver a signed status response during the connection, reducing a client’s direct query to the status service. A client that continues when status checking is unavailable makes a different availability/security tradeoff from one that rejects the connection. Pinning restricts accepted keys or certificates further, while requiring a safe rollover and recovery plan.
example: Assume a client requires TLS 1.2 or newer, validates shop.example correctly and has no compromised keys or implementation flaws. An attacker can drop packets and present a TLS 1.1-only endpoint. The required minimum prevents that session from completing. If a different client explicitly permits legacy fallback, analyze the newly negotiated suite and its specific weaknesses before claiming any plaintext recovery.

questions.prompt: A client previously used TLS 1.2 and is now induced to connect using TLS 1.1. Is that information enough to conclude the attacker can read arbitrary application data? State the missing inputs needed for a defensible analysis.
questions.hint: Identify the concrete record protection and the attacker’s access to keys, oracles and endpoints.
questions.answer: The version change establishes use of a deprecated protocol, while arbitrary plaintext recovery requires a further capability or flaw. Determine the negotiated cipher suite, key exchange, certificate/identity validation, exact fallback path, implementation behavior and the attacker’s position and available oracles. Those inputs define which attacks apply.

questions.prompt: A visitor has a valid saved HSTS policy for shop.example. An attacker poisons DNS to send the visitor to an unrelated server with a valid certificate only for thief.example. Which checks constrain the attack, and which service effect can the attacker still cause?
questions.hint: Evaluate HTTPS selection first and server-name authentication second.
questions.answer: HSTS requires HTTPS, and server-name validation rejects the unrelated certificate for shop.example. The attacker can still deny access by redirecting or dropping traffic. An accepted impersonating HTTPS endpoint would require an additional credential or validation compromise.

title: QUIC streams, migration and amplification
heading: Connect encrypted transport state while checking a new network path
problem: a QUIC connection carrying independent streams while its peer changes network address and proves reachability on the new path.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='quic-transport-title' viewBox='0 0 720 407'><title id='quic-transport-title'>Connect encrypted transport state while checking a new network path</title><g font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' fill='#17343d' font-size='19'><rect x='22' y='18' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='43' font-weight='600'>TLS 1.3 handshake inside QUIC over UDP</text><text x='40' y='67' font-size='17'>Authenticate server and derive packet-protection keys</text><path d='M360 81 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='96' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='121' font-weight='600'>Independent ordered streams</text><text x='40' y='145' font-size='17'>A missing byte blocks delivery within its own stream</text><path d='M360 159 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='174' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='199' font-weight='600'>Connection ID locates existing connection state</text><text x='40' y='223' font-size='17'>Authenticated packets can arrive from a changed address</text><path d='M360 237 v12 m-5 -5 l5 5 l5 -5' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='22' y='252' width='676' height='62' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='40' y='277' font-weight='600'>Validate the new path and respect send limits</text><text x='40' y='301' font-size='17'>PATH_CHALLENGE/RESPONSE and the pre-validation budget apply</text><text x='360' y='388' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Streams share congestion control and connection resources.</text></g></svg>
explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes requests over one TCP byte stream. A missing TCP segment can delay delivery of all later stream bytes even when they belong to unrelated requests. QUIC places multiple reliable ordered streams inside an encrypted transport over UDP. Loss on one stream can leave data on another stream deliverable, while both still share congestion control, network capacity and connection-level flow control.

QUIC integrates the TLS 1.3 handshake with transport setup. In a successful ordinary new connection without retry or loss, the client can send a request after one round-trip time (RTT). A simplified TCP plus TLS 1.3 setup normally needs one RTT for TCP and another for TLS before that request; TLS 1.2 can add another RTT. DNS, application processing, retry and loss are separate costs. Resumption can permit 0-RTT early data, whose replay risk requires application-specific handling.

A QUIC packet carries frames such as STREAM, ACK and connection-management frames. Packet numbers support acknowledgement and loss detection; stream offsets identify bytes within each stream. Retransmission sends lost information in new packets with new packet numbers. This separates transport packet history from the application’s stream byte positions.

The destination connection ID helps a receiving endpoint find existing connection state after a NAT rebinding or address migration. Possession of a visible ID alone does not authenticate a packet. Established packet protection authenticates it, and path validation checks whether the peer can receive at its claimed new address. A PATH_CHALLENGE carries unpredictable data that the peer returns in PATH_RESPONSE.

Before validating a client address, a server’s cumulative send limit is three times the bytes it has received from that address. If R is received bytes and S is bytes already sent while the limit applies, the remaining budget is max(0, 3R − S) bytes. This limits reflection toward spoofed addresses. A valid address-validation token can establish reachability earlier; after validation, congestion control and flow control still constrain sending. Fig. 2 varies the pre-validation accounting rather than simulating a complete QUIC stack.

QUIC Initial packet keys are derived from public inputs, including a version-specific salt and the client’s Initial destination connection ID. They provide a consistent protected packet format but allow an observer to recover Initial contents. Later handshake and application keys rely on the TLS exchange. A Retry can require a new Initial destination connection ID and new Initial keys. Thus a packet’s encryption level and handshake stage matter when assessing confidentiality.

QUIC carries its transport inside UDP so applications can update it in user space. Encrypting most transport details limits middleboxes’ ability to depend on those details, reducing protocol ossification: old network assumptions that obstruct later changes. A browser can discover HTTP/3 through Alt-Svc or HTTPS DNS records. When the path blocks UDP or QUIC fails, a supporting application can fall back to HTTP over TCP/TLS. Discovery, reachability and fallback are operational choices around the protected session.
example: An unvalidated address has sent the server R = 1400 bytes. The server has already sent S = 2600 bytes. Its remaining anti-amplification budget is 3×1400 − 2600 = 1600 bytes. A planned 2000-byte flight must wait, fit within the remaining allowance, or follow successful address validation. The calculation uses cumulative QUIC-accounted datagram bytes, with no assumed packet loss.

questions.prompt: An unvalidated peer has supplied 1200 bytes and the server has sent 3000 bytes. Can the server immediately send another 900 bytes under the 3× rule? How much additional received data would make that flight fit, ignoring packet-size constraints?
questions.hint: Compute the remaining cumulative allowance before considering a new flight.
questions.answer: The allowance is 3600 bytes total, leaving 600. A 900-byte flight would raise sent bytes to 3900. The server needs R ≥ 3900/3 = 1300, so at least 100 additional received bytes, or successful address validation, before that flight fits this rule.

questions.prompt: An observer learns a QUIC connection ID and captures Initial packets. Which information can it recover under QUIC’s Initial key derivation, and what additional checks protect migration of an established session?
questions.hint: Separate public Initial key inputs, established packet keys and proof of reachability.
questions.answer: The observer can derive Initial keys from the public version inputs and relevant Initial destination connection ID and recover Initial payloads. Established packet contents require the later TLS-derived keys. Migration uses authenticated connection packets plus new-path reachability checks; the visible connection ID locates state rather than proving peer identity.
